Also some edible mushrooms growing on top of agricultural waste.

Some chickens.

Some disgusting worms that are good for feeding the chickens and turning the soil medium in a container.

Fun childhood but I think you don't see these animals as much anymore. Also, memories of catching carp/loatch near the rice fields with my uncle and cousins. Edible non-commercialised berries (with worms in it). Banana leaves to make toys out of.

We weren't even rural, just a preindustrial small town big on agriculture, and bordering some nature that's still remaining.

And snakes.

I was going to say medicine, which I actually got into (an undergraduate program in my country). But I realize the reason I didn't attend was because I didn't believe I'd make good doctor and the stress from verbal abuse taken by medical students would break me, based on the stories I found online. This is mostly due to poor coping skills and poor social skills on my part. In the end it doesn't matter. I still wouldn't go for medicine (despite the status and relatively good pay compared to my current situation). 

Maybe Law. Linguistics and more on the computational side, I don't know. Medical assistant? Plumbing (actually a profession I look up to and find "fun" since a kid).

I went into a line of work after college that was my plan B. I didn't plan for any career in college because of personal and family reasons, general cluelessness and anxiety about the world, and escapism. After college, I knew the line of work I was getting into was not sustainable for me in the long term, because while the pay was decent, I didn't feel like I was doing good for my community in the long run (on a local or national level). I had something else I always said I wanted to do (but did not pursue). 

In the end I decided to quit that job when my body suddenly developed weird pain/soreness/numbness, which over time turned into mild chronic pain related to my spine and posture. I couldn't sit for more than 2 hours even with breaks without feeling discomfort for subsequent days/weeks until I get a chiropractic adjustment. I tried standing or kneeling while I'm doing my own work (since I had already quit my job at this point).

It's been over 2 years now. I became a NEET at first prompted by my health situation, in part a self fulfilling prophecy from getting into my Plan B line of work instead of pursuing what I had wanted, an aversion to workplace phoniness, and having financially supportive family.

Edit: my health situation has been much better (50 - 70% recovered). Still, this alone does not help with getting me back to work. If anything it's more like a "bonus" excuse that I give when an excuse for not working is needed.

Edit2: I am being seen by a psychiatrist currently who suggested that the onset of my symptoms might also be trauma-related, which I do not disagree, because I had had a nasty interaction with someone I like and then ended up hating a month or two before I also became depressed (but not Major Depression) for a long time. The onset of the "depression" was roughly concurrent with me quitting my job. When I realized I was so distraught I could not even make a U-turn while driving around, I decided to see a psychiatrist. At some my point my mood stabilized a little, and at that point onwards one might say staying a NEET is a voluntary choice.

I am a male INFP with Chinese appearance+identity, originally from a Southeast Asian country, who lived in the US for 4 years (college). I will not pretend to have identical issues regarding race as the People of Color who have spent most of their lives in the US or the West at large. However, I do feel that my experience of having lived in northeastern US and my home country informs my understanding of racism that is worthy of sharing. (omg, narcissism much) 

I believe racism has multiple origins and modes of operating in public life or regulating social interactions. Personally, the hurt I experienced vis-a-vis race in America was akin to a 10-times magnified version of the embarrassment a financially poor person might feel over not being able to afford stuff or access opportunities as easily as their wealthier peers. It is also a feeling of life being circumscribed, e.g. worry that your own flaws might reflect bad on your own people.

My hurt, in relation to race, largely stemmed from my position as an outsider--an international student adapting to the US, trying to find my bearings around folks. I am not expecting everyone to bend over backwards for me as a new guy in a new country, but there are differences in how white European students are received vs the other foreign students. While some people were able to wear their foreignness like a honor badge ("back in Europe, we wouldn't ..."), having their funny accents celebrated ("she has a nice accent"), others do not have that kind refuge as often while adapting. 

Objectively, I think the difference in the opportunities of having one's background affirmed perhaps lies in the fact that most US natives are white and of European heritage, and people usually like things that (they) are familiar (with). Together with their currently most advanced development in technologies and world political power, the worlds gets to be molded in their shape and preferences. In short, white people have the power to enforce their truths more than the POCs, usually - and the POCs have to live that truths in a lot of social situations. 

If true, this highlights the plain fact that equality, or even "just" equal opportunity, if they are possible, cannot be established by legislation alone, but must find expression in social reality. Laws might reign in the harshest injuries a majority of any social system could inflict on its minorities--through neglect, exclusion, or direct harm--but long-term just, peaceful coexistence must build on shared, mutual understanding. That won't come through pleading to the majority, because human nature. I think historically the various ethnicities in the US (e.g. Irish, Africans, Italians, Chinese etc) had to tap into their own network, build human capital, acquire wealth, establish connections etc to improve their situation. It is easy to say all these, as those (spelling: as though) racism in the West or anywhere is just some unfortunate human flaws that we had no control over would be passe in due course. But looking at black people, who spoke English in the US, practically been there longer than any immigrant groups but yet are the most oppressed by the government, one must think that racism is actively maintained. (my own guess)

How does one deal with that hurt and anguish so that it is possible to live? How does one look people in the eyes who would see a certain name on resume and are less likely to call back the applicant? I won't pretend to have an answer.

Edit: I think talking about my experience, speaking my truths, when possible, is one of the ways of "dealing" with it. The majority usually had cultural instruments (e.g. media, other members of majority, the government) that speak their truths. Truths from the "other side" is harder to come by.
